world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

tone_statements.citation: Odera, Hellen Selah. 2021. A morpho-syntactic analysis of tense and aspect in Lutsotso. MA thesis, Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology (Kakamega), 159 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Although this study discusses verb inflection just like the present study, Lutsotso language is non-tonal unlike Chichewa which is a tonal language. ... We notice that the study also identified that tone contrasts and distinctive vowel length play a role in past tense marking unlike in Lutsotso where tense is mainly marked by morphemes.
tone_statements.locator: p. 4, section 1.1 Background to the study; second sentence p. 12, literature review on Kimbeere tense
tone_statements.summary: Author asserts 'non-tonal' (unreliable; contradicted by Dalgish's tone/accent marking and Marlo 2013).

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerry [Gerard M.]. 1975. Nasal interactions and Bantu vowel-initial roots: the morphological or phonological solution? Proceedings of the Sixth Conference on African Linguistics, OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 20: 68-74.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Silent on stress; 'final accented a' (p. 72) refers to the tonal accent of imperatives, not word stress. Data from 10 months with Orren Tsuma, OluTsootso speaker; Guthrie E.32b.

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerry [Gerard M.]. 1974. Arguments for a unified treatment of y-initial and vowel-initial roots in Olutsootso. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 4(2): 76-90.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number P1.S785)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number P1 .S785
sources.note: Nothing about word stress. Only prominence remarks are notational footnotes: fn. 3 'The capitalized segments indicate that raised tone and accent are on that syllable' (p. 89) and fn. 10 'The capitalized and underlined vowels in these paradigms indicate that high tone and accent fall on these vowels, and that all preceding tones must be low' (p. 90) — tonal (H-tone/accent) notation for imperative paradigms, no stress rule.
Phonology section is Luwanga-based; nothing on tone or stress; lists Tsotso only as one of the Luhya-proper dialects.

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143.
sources.note: Tsootso only in fn. 11: 'See Dalgish (1986) for discussion of related phenomena in Tsootso' (vowel shortening). No stress statement; survey of Luyia verbal tone melodies (Bukusu, Idakho, Khayo, Marachi, Nyala-West, Tiriki, Tura, Wanga etc.).

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2013. Verb tone in Bantu languages: micro-typological patterns and research methods. Africana Linguistica 19: 137-234.
sources.note: Tsotso appears only in list (50) 'Tsotso (Dalgish 1974: 85-88)' among languages where Imperative/Subjunctive + OM is a tonally distinct construction, and in the references (Dalgish 1974). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2009. Khayo verbal tonology. Africana Linguistica 15: 77-129.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Khayo, not Tsotso. Single Tsotso mention: 'Some other Luyia dialects, including Marachi and Tsotso, and a number of other Bantu languages have the final vowel -a in this context (Marlo 2008b, Meeussen 1967, Polak 1986)' (Imperative + OP). No stress statement for any variety; 'penultimate' only as tone-docking site.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2008. Tura verbal tonology. Studies in African Linguistics 37(2): 153-243.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Tura (different Luyia variety); no mention of Tsotso at all; not used.

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerard M. 1986. /-a-/ reduction phenomena in Luyia. Studies in African Linguistics 17(2): 155-176.
sources.note: Silent on stress and tone; discusses OluTsootso vowel length (compensatory lengthening, pre-nasal-cluster lengthening) and segmental morphophonemics of the distant-past /-a-/ only.

sources.citation: PHOIBLE 2.0, language page tsot1241 (inventory 'Lutsootso (GM 1441)', 31 segments) and Glottolog 5.3 languoid tsot1241 / reference pages
sources.note: No suprasegmental information; PHOIBLE inventory sourced from Dalgish 1976. Glottolog descriptive refs for Tsotso: Dalgish 1974, 1975, 1976 (+ Kanyoro 1983 as Glottolog's most extensive description).

sources.citation: Odera, Hellen Selah. 2021. A morpho-syntactic analysis of tense and aspect in Lutsotso. MA thesis, Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology (Kakamega), 159 pp.
sources.quote: Although this study discusses verb inflection just like the present study, Lutsotso language is non-tonal unlike Chichewa which is a tonal language. ... We notice that the study also identified that tone contrasts and distinctive vowel length play a role in past tense marking unlike in Lutsotso where tense is mainly marked by morphemes.
sources.locator: p. 4, section 1.1 Background to the study; second sentence p. 12, literature review on Kimbeere tense
sources.note: The background chapter asserts that Lutsotso is 'non-tonal' (p. 4) and that tense in Lutsotso is 'mainly marked by morphemes' rather than by tone contrasts and vowel length (p. 12); tone is otherwise not analysed and is listed under further research ('Further research on mood, tone, denial, and quantity would be beneficial since they are not discussed in the study', p. 137). Data are cited in orthography without tone marks. sources.note: Only other Tsotso-specific thesis located; a Kenyan MA typically opens with a language-background chapter that may repeat a stress/tone remark, but the topic is sociolinguistic so the chance is low.

sources.citation: Kanyoro, Rachel Msimbi Angogo. 1983. Unity in diversity: a linguistic survey of the Abaluyia of western Kenya. Wien: Afro-Pub (Beiträge zur Afrikanistik), 322 pp. [publication of her 1980 University of Texas at Austin PhD dissertation]

sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Comparative/dialect survey covering all Luyia varieties including Tsotso (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description, 7 pp. on Tsotso); a comparative phonology overview may contain a general statement on Luyia tone vs. stress applicable to Tsotso.

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerard Matthew. 1976. The morphophonemics of the OluTsootso dialect of (Olu)Luyia: issues and implications. PhD dissertation, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, vi+255 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: The only full phonology of Tsotso (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a phonology; source of PHOIBLE's Lutsootso inventory); if any statement on stress/accent vs. tone exists for Tsotso it is here, presumably in the introductory chapter on the sound system and in the treatment of vowel length and tone.
